> **[case-study]**
> **Halcott Roasters**
> 
> Halcott Roasters buys green coffee beans, roasts them and sells ground coffee to independent cafés in country D. It can roast 80,000 kg a year and is currently roasting 62,000 kg.
> 
> Cafés pay \$11.00 per kg. The variable cost of each kg is \$6.40. Fixed costs are \$260,000 a year.
> 
> Verrow Hotels has offered Halcott a one-off order for 15,000 kg at \$8.20 per kg. The coffee would carry Verrow's own label, which would add \$0.90 to the variable cost of every kg in the order.
> 
> The finance director has calculated that the order would add \$13,500 to annual profit and points out that Halcott has the spare capacity to roast it.
> 
> The marketing director is less certain. Verrow runs 40 hotels in the region and has said it would expect the same price on any repeat order. Two of Halcott's café customers have recently asked for a discount. The sales manager also forecasts that café orders will grow by 12% next year.

Evaluate whether Halcott Roasters should accept the one-off order from Verrow Hotels.
parts.solution_md:
Contribution costing compares the extra revenue an order brings in with the extra variable costs it causes **[K]**. Verrow would pay \$8.20 per kg against a variable cost of \$7.30 once own-label packaging is included **[Ap]**. Each kg therefore contributes \$0.90, and 15,000 kg would add \$13,500 **[An]**. Because Halcott has 18,000 kg of spare capacity, the \$260,000 of fixed costs is already being paid whether or not the order is taken, so the whole \$13,500 falls through to profit **[An]**. Set against a current profit of \$25,200, that is an increase of more than half for output the business would not otherwise be producing **[An]**

The difficulty is that the order is unlikely to remain one-off **[K]**. Verrow runs 40 hotels and has already said it would expect \$8.20 again **[Ap]**. At that price a kg earns \$0.90 rather than the \$4.60 a café pays, and once café orders grow by the forecast 12% to 69,440 kg, the 80,000 kg capacity could not hold both **[An]**. Halcott would then be choosing between them, and every kg switched from a café to Verrow would cost \$3.70 in lost contribution **[An]**

There is also a risk to existing prices **[K]**. Two cafés have already asked for a discount **[Ap]**. If they discover that a hotel chain buys the same coffee for \$8.20, holding the \$11.00 price becomes harder, and because contribution per kg is high a small general discount would wipe out the gain; a cut of just \$0.25 across 62,000 kg removes \$15,500, more than the order earns **[An]**

Halcott should accept, but only on terms that keep the order genuinely one-off **[E]**. The arithmetic holds while capacity is spare, and \$13,500 for coffee that would otherwise not be roasted is worth having **[E]**. What makes the decision risky is not the price but what the price implies about the future, since contribution costing answers only the question of this order and says nothing about the next one **[E]**. The order should be agreed in writing as a single delivery with no guarantee on repeat pricing, and own-label work used to fill capacity only while café demand sits below forecast **[E]**. If Verrow will not accept those terms the order should be declined, because a permanent \$0.90 customer displacing \$4.60 customers would leave Halcott busier and poorer **[E]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** limitation of contribution costing.
parts.solution_md:
Contribution costing calculates the contribution a product makes by subtracting only its variable costs from its selling price **[1]**. Because fixed costs are not allocated to individual products, a product showing a positive contribution appears worthwhile even when it may not be **[1]**. If a business accepts too many orders priced only slightly above variable cost, total contribution may fail to cover its fixed costs, so it can make an overall loss while every individual product still appears to be contributing **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Contribution costing subtracts only variable costs from selling price, leaving fixed costs unallocated
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A positive contribution does not guarantee the product is profitable once fixed costs are considered
> - Accepting many low-contribution orders can leave total contribution below total fixed costs
> - Fixed costs still have to be recovered from somewhere, so ignoring them only defers the question
> - Contribution costing gives no guide to long-term pricing, since a price above variable cost may be unsustainable
> - Splitting costs into fixed and variable is not always straightforward, and some costs are partly both
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A limitation has to show where the method can mislead, not merely what it leaves out. "It ignores fixed costs" describes how contribution costing works; the limitation is that ignoring them can produce a decision that turns out to be wrong. Take the extra step to the bad decision and the mark follows.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **way that a business may reduce its variable costs.
parts.solution_md:
A business could reduce its variable costs by buying raw materials in bulk to get a discount** [1]**. For example, a bakery could order larger amounts of flour less often to negotiate a lower price per bag** [1]**. This would reduce the cost of making each item, which could increase the business's profit margin** [1]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **use of break-even analysis.
parts.solution_md:
Break-even analysis can help a business decide whether to launch a new product **[1]**. For example, it can show how many units the business would need to sell to cover its costs **[1]**. If this number seems too high compared to expected demand, the business can decide not to launch the product, avoiding a risky and possibly unprofitable decision **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks

> 
> AO1
> 
> - Break-even analysis can be used to help a business decide whether to launch a new product, by showing how many units it would need to sell to cover its costs.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - For example, a business considering launching a new product could use break-even analysis to calculate the number of units it would need to sell before making a profit, helping it judge whether this target is realistic given expected demand.
> - If the break-even output looks too high compared to likely sales, the business could decide not to go ahead with the product, avoiding a costly decision that would be unlikely to become profitable.
>

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'break-even point'.
parts.solution_md:
The break-even point is the level of output where a business's total revenue equals its total costs **[1]**, so it makes neither a profit nor a loss **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The level of output/sales at which total revenue equals total costs, meaning the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
> - The point at which a business's income from sales is exactly equal to its total costs.
> - The output level a business must reach before it starts making a profit, where total costs and total revenue are the same

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose a mark by simply writing "the point where a business makes no profit or loss" without explaining why — i.e. that total revenue equals total costs. Make sure your definition includes both the cause (revenue equals costs) and the effect (no profit or loss) to secure full marks. Avoid vague language such as "the business breaks even" — this is circular and does not demonstrate understanding of the concept.

parts.problem_md: Analyse **two ways **cost information can be used to monitor and improve the performance of a business.
parts.solution_md:
One way is comparing actual costs against budgeted costs to identify variances **[K]**. For example, a manufacturing business might notice its material costs were much higher than budgeted one month **[Ap]**. This allows managers to investigate the cause, such as a price rise from a supplier **[An]**. If the cause is found quickly, the business can switch to a cheaper supplier before the higher costs damage profit over a longer period **[An]** Another way is using cost information to benchmark performance against competitors **[K]**. A retailer could compare its unit costs with a similar competitor to see if it is running efficiently **[Ap]**. If its costs are higher, this could prompt a review of its processes, such as its supply chain or staffing levels **[An]**. **Jan Guiding Service (JGS) **

Jan loves being in the countryside. Many years ago, he visited country P, where mountains take up 80% of the land area. Country P is one of the poorest countries in the world, with very low income per head. Jan made his home there and took a job assisting with walking groups. He gained a certificate as a professional mountain walking guide. The start of JGS Five years ago Jan set up JGS, in partnership with Gorl, another professional mountain walking guide. JGS offers mountain walking tours. JGS organises and promotes these tours. Originally, Jan and Gorl guided most of the walking tours themselves. JGS has always outsourced all its travel and accommodation. Jan and Gorl are spending more time on managing the business and less time guiding as the demand for JGS tours increases. JGS now outsources most of its mountain guiding. Customers stay with host families in mountain villages, most of which cannot be reached by road. Host families are paid by JGS to provide food and accommodation for its customers. Many families compete to provide these services to JGS. Using outsourcing in this way gives JGS many benefits. JGS employs an administrator to organise outsourcing. JGS is one of the few businesses operating in this market. However, Jan knows that other businesses are becoming interested in offering mountain walking tours. Demand for JGS services JGS has not increased its prices for three years. Over 95% of JGS customers are visitors from country K. Demand for JGS tours is increasing and Jan thinks that income levels in country K are an important factor. Average income in country K rose by 5% in 2019. Demand for JGS tours from residents of country K increased by 20% in the same period. Jan currently believes that there is still time to get more bookings for quarters 3 and 4 in 2020. He also knows that increasing the effectiveness of the JGS Internet presence is important. Gorl has analysed sales figures for the last three years. Table 1 shows his results. He has used the moving average method and has forecast the centred moving average (trend) sales figure for Quarter 3 2021 of \$86560.

Additional opportunities for growth Jan and Gorl are always aiming to expand JGS. They are enthusiastic about the future and are considering two growth options. parts.problem_md: Discuss the importance of accurate cost information to managers of a small business.
parts.solution_md:
Accurate cost information is important because it lets managers monitor changes in specific costs **[K]**. For example, a small furniture maker could notice that the price of wood has increased **[Ap]** and switch to a cheaper supplier before this seriously affects profit. Without this information, a small business might not notice rising costs until it is already losing money, which is especially risky for a small business with limited cash reserves **[An]**

It is also important for setting the right price **[K]**. A small café that miscalculates its costs might set prices too low **[Ap]**, eating into its profit, or too high, making it less competitive than bigger rivals. Since small businesses often cannot benefit from the same economies of scale as larger competitors, controlling and understanding costs is one of the few ways they can stay price competitive **[An]**

Overall, I think accurate cost information is very important for most small businesses **[E]**, as they usually have less financial cushion to survive mistakes than larger businesses **[Ap]**. However, its importance may be lower for a small business with a strong USP, where customers are willing to pay a premium regardless of price **[Ap]**, so cost control, while still useful, may matter slightly less than factors like quality or customer service **[E]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Accurate cost information allows managers to monitor trends in specific costs, such as raw materials
> 
>   - For example, a small furniture maker could spot that wood prices have risen sharply and switch to a cheaper supplier before the increase seriously damages its profit margin.
> - Cost information allows managers to check whether spending is staying within budget - a small café owner could use this to see if ingredient costs are exceeding what was planned, allowing them to take corrective action, such as adjusting portion sizes or menu prices, before losses build up over several months.
> - Accurate cost information is essential for setting the right price - a small business that miscalculates its costs might set a price too low to cover expenses, eating into profit, or too high, making it less competitive against larger rivals; getting this right is especially important for a small business with limited cash reserves to absorb mistakes.
> - Small businesses often struggle to compete with larger businesses, which benefit from economies of scale and lower unit costs
> 
>   - Accurate cost monitoring can help a small business control and reduce its own costs where possible, helping it stay price competitive even without the same scale advantages.
> 
> Evaluation:
> 
> - Accurate cost information is likely to be very important for a small business, since it typically has less financial cushion than a larger business to absorb the impact of pricing or budgeting mistakes.
> 
> - However, its importance may depend on how the business competes — if a small business has developed a strong unique selling point (USP), customers may be less price-sensitive, meaning cost control (though still useful) may matter less than for a business competing mainly on price.
> 
> - It could also be argued that cost information is only one part of good management — factors like quality, customer service and marketing may be equally important to a small business's overall success.
> 
> - Overall, accurate cost information is likely to be essential for most small businesses to survive and remain competitive, but its relative importance depends on the specific market and strategy the business is using to compete.
